## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Karim and Ingrid both want proof on their own calls before paying, so they belong together under a plain name; Andreas, who already knows his numbers and finds the licence too dear, and Hannes, who refuses at any price, rightly stand alone.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line; even Hannes's flat refusal is an on-topic answer about price, and nothing off-topic was put in a group.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea, who pays and sending, but 'Offer a pilot?' (22) comes after I had already set my €3,000 money-back pilot as the first real step (20–21), so it reads as a late afterthought rather than part of how it sells.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the same kicker and the same question; and the pilot is asked at 20–21 (the commitment step, which for me is the paid pilot at one hotel) and again at 22 ('Offer a pilot?').
founder.missing: A way to state two prices: the one-off €3,000 pilot fee and the recurring per-hotel monthly licence that follows roll-out. Also the pilot's terms that make it low-risk: money-back if it does not pay off, and the fee credited to the account on roll-out.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It moves from how many calls we lose, to what it is worth, who pays and signs, how long the review takes, and only then whether I would run a pilot, which is how I would think it through myself.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 6 and 7 overlap a little: the data protection review time and then what would take the time in buying, though 7 does dig into my answer rather than repeat it.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: How we cover those calls today and what that costs us (night staff, an outside call center), whether it connects to our reservation and property systems so a call becomes a real booking, and which languages it handles for our guests; also screen 3 quotes a monthly figure of €1,000 to €2,500 that I was never actually asked for.

screens.why1: Right after naming who else has to agree, asking what my hotel group buyers must clear before paying is the obvious next step of how it sells.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain to me, and the example and the 'not your own trial or pilot' line tell me exactly what kind of step to type.
screens.why3: I know these gates from selling to German hotel groups: the data protection review of recorded guest calls and the PMS check are what I meet in every deal.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with a single escape, 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a founder who cannot name a step.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my 'data protection review of guest calls' word for word, but it says 'about 4 weeks', a time I never typed.
screens.why7: The belief already carries 'within about 4 weeks' before I have typed any time, and the card says a time the founder never typed is the edge the whole scale turns on, so it measures nothing; a correct screen would also have flagged my 'A trial at one hotel first' as my own pilot rather than a buyer-side step.
screens.instead: Same question and hint, with the belief left without a time until I type it ('Most hotel group revenue directors would get through a data protection review of guest calls within about ___, or not need it'), and my 'trial at one hotel first' flagged as my own pilot.

screens.why1: Right after I named who must agree, it makes sense to check the steps my buyer's side has to clear before paying for Codyco.
screens.why2: Data protection review, works council and PMS are everyday words in a German hotel group, so I read every row on first pass.
screens.why3: These are the gates I hit with every hotel group I sell to: the DSGVO review of recorded guest calls, the Betriebsrat on call handling, and checking the PMS write-through.
screens.why4: The three steps are real and distinct, but the fourth 'row' is a long explanatory sentence shown as if it were a step, and 'a check that bookings land in our PMS' is close to the integration my pitch says it handles, so it is half a step I remove.
screens.why5: The steps keep my words, but the belief already says 'about 4 weeks', a time I never typed, so it speaks for me on the one number the scale turns on.
screens.why7: The belief carries 'within about 4 weeks' before I have typed any time, and the card says a time the founder never typed makes the band edge no one's belief, which breaks the dimension.
screens.instead: Same three rows with the note moved out of the list, and a belief with no time yet: 'Most hotel group revenue directors would get through a data protection review of guest calls within about [your time], or not need it.'

screens.why1: Right after I checked the steps Keel wrote, this is the obvious place to pick the one brake to test and give it my time.
screens.why2: Data protection review, works council and PMS are everyday words in a German hotel group, and the time box is plain.
screens.why3: I know how long a data protection review of recorded guest calls takes at the groups I sell to, so 4 weeks is my own estimate, not a guess about someone else's job.
screens.why4: The data protection and works council rows are real buyer-side gates in Germany, but 'a check that bookings land in our PMS' is really my own integration and onboarding, not a brake the hotel's own process imposes.
screens.why5: My step is kept in my words, and the belief carries the 4 weeks I typed, not a time Keel supplied.
screens.why7: My own step and typed time make the edge and the bar (at least 2 in 3 under 4 weeks or not needed) can hold or fail, but the intro still frames the stranger's question as 'how long would this step take before it went through', which the card forbids, and the PMS row is close to my own onboarding.
screens.instead: Intro: 'The person who decides gets one question: if they bought it, how long would this step take?' Rows: A data protection review of guest calls · A works council review of call handling · A sign-off from the hotel's owner.

screens.why1: After who decides and what they must clear, asking for the first paid step is the natural last commercial question, and for me that is the €3,000 pilot.
screens.why2: "First real step", "pilot" and "what would it cost them" are how I already talk to hotel groups, and the hint's examples match my zero-risk pilot exactly.
screens.why3: The pilot terms are my own offer, so I can answer from what I sell every week.
screens.why4: The only chip is the founder's escape, "Leave this out of the study", which fits the card's *I'm not sure* allowance on the founder side, and it is worded plainly.
screens.why5: I typed "pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel", but the belief says "pay for a money-back pilot at one hotel" and drops the €3,000, which is what the director is actually agreeing to.
screens.why7: The belief follows the decider's template and keeps the money-back and one-hotel terms, but it cuts the number I wrote, a defining term the card says to keep (the euro-sign pitfall), even though the step fits in 9 words with it.
screens.instead: Keep the question and hint as they are; write the belief as "In most cases the hotel group revenue director would pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel."

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first step, a check of how strangers will hear it is exactly where this belongs before the frame closes.
screens.why2: "Pay for a money-back pilot at one hotel" is how a hotel group revenue director talks, with no word from outside the trade.
screens.why3: It is my own step and my own terms from the partnership page, so I can judge it at once.
screens.why4: The step costs money, so a free smaller step should sit beside it for the soft yes, but none is visible in what the screen shows, so I cannot confirm the list is complete.
screens.why5: I wrote "pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel", which fits in nine words, but Keel dropped the €3,000, the very number that tells the director what he is agreeing to.
screens.why7: The step and the decider's belief fit the measure, but the card says to keep every term that changes the agreement, including the euro sign, and the price was cut although it fitted under nine words.
screens.instead: Step: pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel; smaller step: a free 10-minute call with us first. Options: Yes, I'd pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel · Probably, after a free 10-minute call with us first · Probably not · No.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the right moment to decide whether strangers get a pilot ask, and it follows directly from the Commitment step I set on the previous screens.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with a yes or no is plain to me; a pilot is how I sell to hotel groups, and the Pilot tab is self-explanatory.
screens.why3: Whether I want to collect pilot leads from this study is my own decision, and I can answer it at once.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover the choice, they are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: My step is a paid €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel, but the line strangers will see is a free-sounding "try this for real? Leave your email" that drops the price, and the step saved here has already lost its €3,000.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one of your hotels? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the link goes out, after the study and the pilot offer are settled.
screens.why2: It is mostly plain, but the hint mixes 'voice', 'video' and 'face', and the recorded pick says 'face', so I have to read it twice to know whether I am picking a voice, a face or both.
screens.why3: As the founder I know how my reservation agents would take a stranger's call, so I can judge which interviewer suits them.
screens.why4: The two voices are distinct and each has a 5-second preview, but nothing says what language they speak, and my respondents are reservation agents in Germany who should hear the questions in German.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco's product or roles leaks here, and 'reservation agents' is my own word for who answers.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, in German? Daphne (German, ▶ hear 5 s) / Saskia (German, ▶ hear 5 s). The voice and face you pick are recorded once for this project, 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the reservation agents, it is natural to choose how the revenue directors on the commercial link answer, one screen before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words, and each option says what the director would see and do, so Daphne needs no prior explanation.
screens.why3: I know my directors are busy people on a phone or laptop, so I can judge whether they would sit through a video or tap through.
screens.why4: The options are complete and distinct: video AI, text, or the respondent's choice, which covers every real way to send it.
screens.why5: 'Directors' is a fair short form of the hotel group revenue director I named, and nothing of Codyco leaks into the format choice.
screens.instead: How should the revenue directors answer? (AI interviewer · Daphne / Read and tap / Let them choose)

screens.why1: After choosing how directors answer, the obvious last step is deciding who receives the link, and it comes at the right point of sending.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'Contacts page' and 'signs in with Google' are clear to a founder who has been using Keel, and each option is one idea.
screens.why3: I know which hotel group revenue directors I can reach by name: the seven groups we work with and the people who booked calls after our launch.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search list and one open link in a group cover how I would reach directors; they are distinct and each has a one-line explanation.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks and my pick is kept, but 'Who gets a link?' does not say whether this is the directors' link or the reservation agents' link, and I am sending both.
screens.instead: Who gets the revenue directors' link? -- People I know by name / People I found with Keel / A group, with one open link

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits right under the title with the deciding card and its count, Purchase friction at 4 of 8 under 4 weeks; the card below adds the bar of 6 of 8, so I know which belief sank the stage and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives its count and its bar, but the kicker's '4 TO 8 COUNTED' and Ability to pay's '4 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed' make me stop and work out who was counted and what the 5 is a bar of.
screens.why_b3: The three beliefs I checked (Buyer and payer, Purchase friction, Commitment) are word for word what I approved, and the other three carry my own numbers: 5% of calls, €3,000 up front, €1,000 per hotel a month.
screens.why_b4: The only statement under the verdict says who answered, not what to do; nothing tells me to put a GDPR or data-processing pack in front of the directors before the pilot, or to look again at the €1,000 licence that only half accept.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible on every card and nothing at the bar is called strong, but 8 directors is a small sample and the screen never says so, while 'Holding up' on Commitment at exactly 6 of 8 reads firmer than one person's margin can carry.
screens.instead: Did not hold: only 4 of 8 directors expect the data protection review of guest calls to clear within 4 weeks (bar 6), most say 4 weeks to 3 months, so ship a ready DPA and data-processing answer with the pilot offer; price is split at 4 of 8, and with 8 people every call here is thin.

screens.why_b1: The 4 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, 1 short, sits right beside the status, but the status says 'People disagree a split' rather than plainly saying my belief did not hold, so I have to work out the verdict from '1 short'.
screens.why_b2: The strip is clear about what it counts (% of reservation calls per hotel a month, 7 counted), but '5' appears both as my 5% marker on the axis and as the '5 of 7' bar, so I need a second look to tell where the bar sits.
screens.why_b3: The belief line is my own: about 5% of reservation calls per hotel a month, rung out after hours, at peak or on a holiday, and the question asks the directors exactly that.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats '1 short' and sends me to the Price card, but it doesn't say what this means for the pitch, such as leading with the high-season and resort groups at 8 to 10% rather than groups whose call center already covers after hours.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, Karim's 'can't recall' and Hannes's 0 are both explained, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps the split from being oversold.
screens.instead: Did not hold, just: 4 of 7 directors lose 5% or more of reservation calls a month (bar 5 of 7). The ones above you run resorts or peak-heavy hotels, and the ones below have a call center covering after hours, so lead with the first group.

screens.why_b1: The status and its count sit together: 4 of 8 at my €3,000 up front and 4 of 8 at my €1,000 a month, against a bar of 6 of 8, so 2 short, and it plainly did not reach my bar.
screens.why_b2: The two ladders, my low edges and the 6-of-8 marker are clear, but the second strip shows 4 for and 3 against out of 8 counted, so I have to work out that Hannes's would-not-pay is missing from the monthly side.
screens.why_b3: Price and €3,000 then €1,000 are mine, but my money-back pilot at one hotel credited on roll-out and my €1,000 to €1,500 range are cut down to a bare up-front fee and a single €1,000 figure.
screens.why_b4: Saying 2 short and sending me to the Insights tab is generic; the quotes beside it (Andreas's 4% on nine hotels, Ingrid's call center, Karim's free test number) point at concrete moves the So line never names.
screens.why_b5: n of 8 stays visible, the small group is flagged as a lean rather than a call, and nothing claims more than the eight answers carry.
screens.instead: 4 of 8 would pay €3,000 for the pilot and €1,000 a hotel a month, 2 short of 6; the 4 below have few missed calls or cannot see them, so prove the missed bookings on their own numbers before pricing, and count Hannes against on both strips.

screens.why_b1: The verdict *Too few to call* sits right beside the number that decides it, *4 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed*, so I know there is no answer yet and why.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count where the money would come from for the 4 directors at my price, but the strip's *4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)*, with a ghost cell beside *4 answered*, takes a second look before I see it means 4 of a needed 5. The rule line also leaves out *charged to the teams or sites* and grants, which the chart does mark, and it names a *none* that is not on the chart.
screens.why_b3: The €3,000 up front and €1,000 per hotel a month are my numbers and *Ability to pay* is plain, but I never checked this line on the way in: Keel derived it, and the card calls it *your belief* without saying Keel wrote it.
screens.why_b4: *Waits until 5 have* tells me I need one more director at my price, but it does not tie this to the failing Price card (only 4 of 8 reached €3,000) or say what a 3-for, 1-against lean suggests I do about the pilot fee.
screens.why_b5: It makes no claim past the 4 who were asked: n stays visible, the small group is called *a lean, not a call*, and the 4 not asked are listed with their reasons.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only 4 of 8 directors reached your €3,000 pilot, and 3 of those 4 would pay from a budget line they already have. Reach one more director at your price, or look again at the pilot fee, since half named less. (Keel's reading of your cost and price, not a line you checked.)

screens.why_b1: The verdict *Holding up* sits right beside 6 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, marked *at the bar*, so I know it held, and only just.
screens.why_b2: The four answers are counted in order with for and against on each, over 8 people, and the strip's marker sits at 6, so I can read what is counted, over how many and where the bar is at first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Buyer and payer and carries my belief word for word: the revenue director decides, and the hotel's owner and the finance director must agree first.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for the owner in deals and that 2 of 8 directors could sign alone, and the quote adds that a pilot at one hotel is what got the last tool signed, which fits my pilot.
screens.why_b5: The count line says this is a small group and a lean, not a call, but *Plan for the hotel's owner in most deals* stretches 4 of 8 (half) into most.
screens.instead: Plan for the hotel's owner in about half your deals (4 of 8); 2 of 8 could sign alone, and the finance director was not asked about, so that part of your belief is still untested.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits directly beside the deciding count, 4 of 8 under 4 weeks or not needed against a bar of 6 of 8, 2 short, and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts how long each of the 8 directors expects the review to take, the marker sits at 6, and the label "your 4 weeks is this band's low edge" explains at a glance why the 4-weeks-to-3-months band counts against me.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Purchase friction and repeats my belief word for word: a data protection review of guest calls within about 4 weeks, or not need it.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for a cycle of that length" gives a range of 4 weeks to 3 months but does not say what that does to my €3,000 pilot of up to 8 weeks, for example that the review could use up most of the pilot window unless I start it first.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the count line calls it "a lean, not a call", and every claim stays inside the 4 of 8 who answered.
screens.instead: 4 of 8 expect the data protection review to take 4 weeks to 3 months, longer than your 4 weeks; that can eat most of an 8-week pilot, so have your data processing agreement ready and start the review before the pilot clock runs. The reasons are on the Insights tab.

screens.why_b1: Holding up, with 6 of 8 said yes against a bar of 6 of 8 at the bar, sits right beside the status word, so I know it held and by how little.
screens.why_b2: The four bars count the 8 directors' answers, the strip shows 6 for and 2 against with the marker at 6, and the bar is spelled out as no more than 1 in 3 against; the first bar's label does drop 'at one hotel', but that doesn't slow the read.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and 'In most cases the hotel group revenue director would pay for a money-back pilot at one hotel' are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is a concrete step, but it ignores what I read two cards back: the step was asked without my €3,000, and the Price card had only 4 of 8 at €3,000 up front, so I don't know whether to book six pilots or fix the price first.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly says 'a lean, not a call', but the So line then acts on an exact-at-bar 6 of 8 as settled, and '6 of 8 would pay' reads as more than a yes to an unpriced pilot can carry.
screens.instead: 6 of 8 would take a money-back pilot at one hotel, exactly at your bar and in a small group, but the step named no price and only 4 of 8 took €3,000 up front: offer the pilot to those six with the €3,000 said out loud and see who still signs.

screens.why_b1: Each box names its verdict with the deciding count beside it: Price split 4 of 8 on each rung, Purchase friction did not hold at 4 of 8 against a bar of 6, and Buyer and payer held at 6 of 8, right at the bar.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked: €3,000 up front then €1,000 per hotel a month, the data protection review within about 4 weeks, and the revenue director deciding with the owner and finance director agreeing.
screens.why_b4: The screen is headed 'When a line fails' but never says what to change; I have to infer from the price theme that directors want their own missed-call numbers before paying, and the failed friction line, the one that sank the stage, has no why and no next step.
screens.why_b5: Counts stay visible and nothing is called strong, but the Buyer and payer box promises 'the 2 who said no' and shows one, and that one is Joanna saying her managing director would agree quickly, under an 'against' tag that reads the opposite of her words.
screens.why_b6: Andreas's arithmetic (4% missed across nine hotels makes a €1,000 licence cost more than the bookings it saves), Ingrid's after-hours call center shrinking the loss, Karim not knowing his rate, and Hannes's reputation fear are all things I did not type, and they tell me my price only works where the miss rate is at or above my 5%.

screens.why1: Showing me the idea before the buying questions makes sense, since everything after it asks whether my group would buy this, and the missed calls on late shifts and holidays are exactly what I'd be weighing it against.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot, Apaleo and handing a call to the desk are everyday words in my job, so I follow it on first reading.
screens.why3: I know how many calls our central reservations office misses after hours and at peak, which PMS our hotels run and what routing rules I'd want, so I can judge this from my own operation.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea to consider, it stays on the missed reservation calls, and nothing in it reads like someone else's internal terms for me or my agents.
screens.why6: It says well overall, but the how runs to six sentences instead of one line, the PMS list is a mouthful to hear in one go, and 'nobody picks up' is heard three times.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent that takes the calls nobody picks up. Your hotels forward unanswered calls to it; it answers in the hotel's voice, takes the booking and payment, and writes it into your PMS, handing calls to the desk by your rules. The people building it believe it would take the reservation calls nobody picks up.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking how many of our booking calls went unanswered is the obvious first question about what the problem already costs my group.
screens.why2: 'Rang out' is our trade's word, but I would need a second read to tell whether this means a share of all last month's calls, or a share of only the after-hours, peak and holiday calls.
screens.why3: Our call-center reports give me the unanswered rate each month, about 6% for us, so I can answer from what I see.
screens.why4: One percent box with a plain label, None as zero, and I can't recall as the escape covers every answer I could give.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'calls that don't get answered on every shift, after hours, at peak and on holidays' in our words, and nothing of the product or its roles reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard once it is one short question with one unit and one escape; the list 'after hours, at peak or on a holiday' is three short words a listener can hold.
screens.why7: The box uses the rate mode: a percent of reservation calls over one month, with 'rang out' as the verb rather than 'lost'; any number can fall above or below the founder's low, and the single required escape is there.
screens.instead: Last month, about what percent of all your reservation calls rang out unanswered? [box] % of the reservation calls last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question on how many calls rang out, asking what it would be worth to me is the obvious next step, and I'm the one who pays for these tools.
screens.why2: 'Up front, per hotel' and then 'a month, per hotel' is how our booking engine and channel manager vendors bill us, so I read it once and know what's meant.
screens.why3: I sign off on setup fees and monthly per-property fees for reservation tools, so I can place a figure from what we already pay, even for a new AI agent.
screens.why4: Both ladders run cleanly from low to high with no overlap, 'I wouldn't pay for this' is a real answer, and 'I can't say' sits apart as the one escape.
screens.why5: Nothing reaches me but the idea card's own line, and an up-front fee followed by a monthly plan per hotel reads as a coherent offer rather than drifted terms.
screens.why6: Each step reads four short options and then a two-way follow-up, so even with the plan step after it I can hold every list I hear.
screens.why7: This is one price first and then a plan, so it rightly uses two money ladders of six in euros per hotel, with bands below and above the middle edges, 'I wouldn't pay for this' as an answer and the single 'I can't say' escape on each step.

screens.why1: Straight after I named my price, asking where that money would come from is the obvious next question for the person who holds the budget.
screens.why2: Budget line, signed off and charged to the sites are how I talk about tools at group level, and the two-part price is read back to me as I gave it.
screens.why3: I own the reservations and revenue tooling budget, so I know exactly whether this would sit in my existing line, be allocated to the hotels or need a new sign-off.
screens.why4: The sources are distinct and the true answers are there, but a grant or outside funding is an odd fit for booking tools at a German hotel group, though it does no harm.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product, plan or terms reaches me here; it only points back to my own price.
screens.why6: One short question, five short sources read as a list I can hold, then one escape; pointing back to the price I just gave avoids reading out two euro ranges.
screens.why7: There are five sources of money in the card's order, three for and two against, each reading after would, with I can't say set apart as the chain item requires.

screens.why1: Right after asking where the money would come from, it is natural to ask whether I can approve it myself or need the owner's agreement.
screens.why2: Sign off and the hotel's owner are everyday words in a hotel group, so I could answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my approval limits and when an owner or asset manager has to agree to spending at a property.
screens.why4: The four answers go from me alone to someone else's call, each is distinct, and I can't say fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but it quotes only €3,000 up front when I said €3,000 to €5,000 plus €1,000 to €2,500 a month, and the monthly part is what decides whether I can sign alone.
screens.why6: One short question with four short options read as a list and one escape; €3,000 per hotel says cleanly.
screens.why7: The options are on the one measure and in the card's order, with the tested role named in the second, two answers for and two against, and I can't say apart.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about €3,000 per hotel up front and €1,000 a month yourself, or would the hotel's owner have to agree? I could sign off myself · The hotel's owner would have to agree · Several people would have to agree · It's someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: After who signs off and where the money comes from, asking what would hold up the purchase is the natural next step.
screens.why2: A data protection review is everyday language for a German hotel group, especially for anything that listens to guest calls.
screens.why3: I have been through data protection checks with our DPO on call recording before, so I know roughly how long one takes here.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover everything, it wouldn't be needed is a real possibility, and I can't tell fits as the one escape.
screens.why5: Only the product name from the idea card appears, and the step is in my own terms, with no pitch or founder jargon.
screens.why6: One short question, four options read at once and then a two-way follow-up; easy to hold when heard.
screens.why7: The step is a buyer-side brake, the bands share one edge exactly at 4 weeks with the band below it as to under, there are three options for and three against, and the one escape is I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after I gave the data protection review 4 weeks to 3 months, asking what would eat that time is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: It hands my own band back to me as I'd say it and asks in plain words, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know what holds this up in our group: our data protection officer, the works council because calls get recorded, and the processing agreement with the vendor.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: Codyco is the name from the idea card I was shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms comes through.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, nothing only the eye can read, so I'd answer it after hearing it once.
screens.instead: You said 4 weeks to 3 months for the data protection review. What would take the time?

screens.why1: After price, budget, sign-off and the data protection review, asking whether I'd actually take a first step is the natural last question of the buying section.
screens.why2: A paid pilot at one hotel with money back and a demo first is how tools get bought in our group; I'd answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I'm the one who would decide whether to pay for a pilot at one of our hotels, so I answer this from my own job.
screens.why4: Firm yes, soft yes after a free demo, probably not and no are distinct and cover my real answers, and a demo on sample data rather than our guests' calls is exactly what I'd ask for first.
screens.why5: The idea card names Codyco on purpose, and *money-back pilot at one hotel* is said the way a vendor would offer it to me, with no odd founder jargon about my agents.
screens.why6: One short balanced question, then four short options I can hold after hearing them once.
screens.why7: The first option says yes to the founder's own paid step in its own verb, with *at one hotel* carried by the stem to keep it within nine words; the soft yes names the free smaller step; two answers sit on each side and there is no escape, so the belief can hold or fail.
